title: Created Sprites for Upcoming Title, but Something's Missing ...
author: Fun_Worry_3079
selftext: I've created the following sprites for my upcoming beat-em-up title and, while I'm happy with the overall aesthetic of the characters, I can't help but feel like something is missing. Perhaps someone here in the community could help me?

comments.author: slipperyslips

But i guess what those people mean is that u could make them more unique looking. Currently they look like generic characters u can find in many different games. Give the some "identity" and personality in their look. Details, clothes and so on.

replies.author: Fun_Worry_3079
replies.body: In other words, think like a character designer and use details (mud on the face to show battle weariness, wrinkles in the clothes to show age, etc.) to make the characters more relatable in some way. Correct?

replies.body: Exactly. Try to make them look unique with details like wrinkles, unique clothes, maybe some unique hairstyles (if its matching with your game). Those characters do not look bad, just too boring right now. If u can fix that, u have good characters.

replies.author: Fairway3Games
replies.body:
I don't think people really know what they mean when they say soulless.  But it's usually a combo of things:

First, AI has a tendency to default to vacant or blank expressions by default.  And that's because lots of assets human created also default to blank and expressionless.  The difference is that AI tends to produce assets that LOOK like they should have an expression.  And so, it's self-defeating and gives the soulless feel.

The druid is a pretty good example of that. She looks like she shold have an expression, but doesn't.

Second, AI tends to pick pretty boring, flat colors. Again, that's because those boring, flat colors are really common even if the real world.  But the boring colors are usually paired with accent colors by humans so that they don't appear completely bland.

Again, your druid is a good example.  Nothing wrong with the green and brown. But that's all there is to it.  No flash of something else.

replies.author: Fun_Worry_3079
replies.body: You plucked a thought straight from my head! I feel like the druid could use with pops of different colors; leave the leaf motif, but give the outfit a little more of a design.

comments.body:
Honestly, I think they look pretty good. Each character looks unique, uniform to your style, and proportional. Adding more flare and accessories to make your character look less "soul less" might muddy up the clean animations when set in a level with other enemies, terrain, and a background. comments.author: ZombiiRot
comments.body: The character designs are pretty bland and generic. They pretty much stick to their stereotypes exactly, with very little variation or twist. So because of this they feel pretty bland or mobile gamey, I guess. I think something that helps with this problem, is to combine to unrelated visual tropes together.

replies.author: Fun_Worry_3079
replies.body: That's not a bad piece of advice. I may have to look into that as I further develop these characters.

replies.author: ZombiiRot
replies.body:
Yeah it could be worth it to watch a few videos on character design to learn the basics! 

Also just try to think of other things besides their characters you can showcase, besides their basic RPG style class. Like what environment are they from, and is this environment unique? Like, maybe instead of making the druid a basic wood elf, you could make her be from the jungle, a snowy forest, the ocean, or the desert. This goes beyond basic biome, as you can also show off the culture these characters are from. Try to add variations besides basic medieval western fantasy. Like, maybe your warrior dragonborn character is from a nordic based country. Or your scholarly character could take inspiration from islamic cultures. 

Finally, it could be worth it to think of interests that go beyond their basic type casting, interests you could incorporate into their design. Like, obviously the druid is going to like nature—but what if she also liked wood carving, and is adorned with different carvings like masks and stuff? That scholarly guy looks like he likes books, but maybe he's also very into fashion and is adorned with expensive silk robes and jewlery. Just to give you a few ideas. 

Combine all these ideas, and you'll probably have pretty unique looking characters!

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
not sure why you need the full turn-around if you are making a beat'em up. 

the proportions dont do you much favor either; it is harder to make the fighting animation read well with these kind of proportions (there are a few classic examples of beat'em up in this proportion so it is possible but I think its harder)

replies.author: Fun_Worry_3079
replies.body:
This is true, but I think the challenge will make developing this game worth it. Most of the animations will be simple movements, but I can see how the proportions would make it difficult to read. 

  
As far as creating turn-arounds go, I was always influenced by the animation industry, so I tend to have that mindset when generating characters. That, and I was using kind of like a "mood board," to help me decide what directions I would want the characters to face (facing away to enter doors, etc.).

replies.author: Fun_Worry_3079
replies.body: Also, I could always render these characters at 2x to make everything more readable, especially after adding any character details.

comments.author: featherless_fiend
comments.body:
After seeing your sprites I instantly thought this is a bad perspective for a top-down game which should have a perspective more like pokemon.

But then I see you say it's a "beat-em-up title", and I have a hard time imagining these guys in a beat-em-up. The issue is you've got chibi characters, beat-em-ups should have more physicality and less static anatomy to their designs. You don't necessarily need to scrap the chibi characters but they should definitely be in fighting stances.

comments.author: AtlaStar
comments.body:
What is missing is the experience that comes from making art and the ability to self critique, which current genAI lacks the ability to do.

Ya got shit side perspectives that dont match the other perspectives, inconsistent pixel sizes, none of the images follow a color palette so you get ass shading and everything looking disjoint from one another, and shitty shading of parts of the hair and clothes of the characters.

If you don't care about having things have a professional look to them, you might be able to prompt some of the issues away...but if you want professional quality you are gonna have to have someone with experience tweak what you have...and there aren't a whole lot of pro AI professionals in the art realm, although they do exist, meaning they'd probably charge more than you're willing to shell out.

If ya'll wanna use AI, whatever, but don't use it as an excuse to not even learn some basics...because if you yourself had just a bit more art knowledge you could have seen the issues yourself.
